setting: a coastal kayak tour company adding winter whale-watching trips (Saltmarsh Paddle Co.)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the winter whale‑watching pitch I’m taking to Maya, our co‑founder and CEO, tomorrow. We plan to start the first trip on 15 Dec 2024 and run three weekly tours (Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday) through 31 Mar 2025. Each tour seats 30 guests at $120 per ticket, and we’re budgeting $45 for fuel, $20 for the guide, and $15 for cold‑weather gear per trip. We assume demand will be similar to our spring season, which averaged 70 % occupancy, so we expect to fill about 21 spots per outing. We’ve allocated $15,000 upfront for extra wetsuits and heated storage lockers. The unknown we haven’t nailed down is the insurance premium for operating in winter conditions; the broker gave a rough range of $2,000–$5,000 for the season. Please give me one recommendation on whether to push ahead, the main ways this could fail, and the pre‑agreed condition that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., a specific profit shortfall or safety metric). Also note any hidden cost or flawed assumption you see.

setting: a regional orchard cooperative launching a cider subscription box (Harrowgate Orchards)
prompt: I’m drafting a pitch for Maya Patel, our board chair, about launching a Harrowgate Orchards cider subscription box. We plan a 12‑month pilot starting 1 Nov 2024 with a price of $45 per box, delivered monthly. The model assumes 7,000 subscribers at launch, a 4 % conversion from the 200,000 website visitors we expect in Q4, and that 80 % will renew after the first year. We’ve budgeted $150,000 for packaging (estimated $0.30 per unit for 500,000 units) and $100,000 for marketing, assuming a $10 cost‑per‑acquisition, which would give us 10,000 new customers. Production capacity is 5,000 boxes per month, but we’re planning to fulfill 7,000 boxes from day one. The expected revenue is $540,000 (7,000 × $45 × 12), and we think logistics will be 15 % of revenue. The unknown is the actual churn rate after the first three months; we have no data for this demographic. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the main ways this plan could fail, and the specific result (e.g., churn exceeding X % or capacity breach) that should trigger us to stop or pivot.

setting: a boutique hotel group converting rooms into monthly co-living units (Pinecrest Stays)
prompt: I need a stress‑test of the proposal I’m taking to Maya Liu, our CEO, next week. Pinecrest Stays has 120 rooms across three downtown properties. The plan is to convert 70% of those rooms into monthly co‑living units, costing $250,000 per conversion, so the total outlay is $21 million (I’m assuming the $250k figure includes all construction, furnishings, and a 5% contingency). We expect an average monthly rent of $2,200, which would give us $37 million in annual revenue if we hit 80% occupancy by Q3 2025. The assumption is that the local market will keep rental rates stable through 2027. The unknown is the exact municipal licensing fee for converting traditional hotel rooms to co‑living, which the city has said will be “determined after an impact study.” Also, we haven’t priced the additional fire‑safety upgrades required for longer‑term occupants; the estimate I have is a vague $1 million total. Please give me one clear recommendation, the main ways this could fail (including any arithmetic or comparison issues you spot), and the specific result—like a sustained occupancy below 55% for six months—that would trigger us to kill or pivot the plan.

setting: a community radio network selling podcast sponsorship packages (Fernbank Radio)
prompt: I need a stress‑test of the “Premium Podcast Sponsor” roll‑out I’m taking to Maya Patel, our Chief Revenue Officer, on Thursday, March 15. The plan is to launch a $5,000‑per‑month tier on May 1, 2025, targeting 10 sponsors for the first six months, which would generate $600,000 in revenue (10 × $5,000 × 12 months). We assume an 80 % renewal rate after the first year and that the average CPM for our 12‑episode quarterly series stays at $25. Production costs are estimated at $2,000 per month, but we haven’t priced the added editorial staff time (about 30 hours per month at $45/hour). The competitive benchmark we cite is a regional TV spot that costs $10,000 for a 30‑second slot, but we didn’t adjust for the fact that TV reaches only 15 % of our core demographic. The unknown is the actual churn rate for podcast sponsors in this niche. Please give Maya a single recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and specify the metric or result that would trigger us to kill the tier (e.g., if renewal falls below X % or revenue after six months is under $200,000).

setting: a mid-size tile manufacturer adding a next-day sample delivery service (Calderon Tile)
prompt: Elena – I need a quick stress‑test of our plan to add a next‑day sample delivery service for Calderon Tile before I bring it to you next week. We’d start the pilot on 2025‑03‑01, offering 12‑inch tile samples shipped within 24 hours. The model assumes we’ll ship 2,000 samples per month at $15 each, which we’ve calculated as $35,000 in revenue (actually $30,000, but the spreadsheet shows $35k). Fixed shipping contracts are $500 per month and we estimate a handling labor cost of $2,200 per month. We expect a 12 % gross margin on the samples, so about $3,600 contribution. The assumption is that 80 % of our B2B leads will request a sample, and we’re ignoring any additional packaging waste or insurance. The unknown is how many competitors will roll out a similar service in the next six months – we have no data on that. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the main ways this could fail (e.g., cost overruns, low uptake, operational bottlenecks), and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or re‑evaluate (e.g., net contribution below $5,000 after three months).

setting: a language-school chain launching an online evening cohort (Zephyrine Languages)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal to launch Zephyrine Languages’ first online evening cohort and need it stress‑tested before I present it to our COO, Maya Patel, on Thursday, 2024‑09‑15. The plan is to pilot the cohort for 90 days starting 2024‑10‑01 with a target of 150 paying students, each paying $200 per month for a three‑month program (projected revenue $90,000). We estimate acquisition cost at $45 per student based on our recent summer‑camp campaign, which brought in 12,000 leads at a 0.8% conversion; I’m assuming the same conversion will hold online, so we budget $6,750 for marketing. The platform we’ve chosen claims it can support 5,000 concurrent users, and we’ve allocated $2,200 for a one‑time integration fee, but we haven’t priced ongoing bandwidth, support staff, or the extra $1,200 we’ll need for a weekend‑class moderator. The biggest unknown is the churn rate for evening‑only online learners. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three main ways this rollout could fail, and the concrete result (e.g., enrollment < 100 after the first month) that should trigger us to stop or pivot. Also point out any hidden risk or arithmetic slip you see.

setting: a veterinary clinic group buying a mobile surgery van (Foxglove Animal Care)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal to present to Maya Patel, our COO, about adding a Foxglove Animal Care mobile surgery van to our veterinary clinic group. We currently operate 7 locations and perform an average of 180 surgeries per month across the network. Foxglove quoted $475,000 for a fully outfitted van, plus $28,000 for a two‑year service contract. They claim we can capture 12% of the 2,200 annual referral surgeries we send to external specialists, which would generate roughly $132,000 in revenue per year (they’ve calculated $11,000 per captured case). My assumption is that each captured case will net $9,500 after consumables and staff overtime, but I haven’t factored the additional $4,200 per month for a dedicated veterinary anesthetist. I also need to know the insurance premium for the mobile unit, which they haven’t disclosed. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and the specific metric (e.g., net profit falling below $45,000 in year 1) that would trigger us to abandon or redesign the project. Keep in mind the potential arithmetic slip in their revenue estimate and the missing cost of the anesthetist.

setting: a craft brewery adding a canning line in-house (Longmeadow Brewing)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the proposal I’m taking to Maya Patel, our CFO, about installing an in‑house canning line at Longmeadow Brewing. I’ve estimated the line will cost $2.5 million, will run at 6,000 cans per hour, and should cut our outsourced canning fees by roughly $300 k per year, giving us a payback in about 8.5 years. We plan to start the build on 1 Mar 2025 and finish in 12 months, then ramp up to 85 % utilization by Q4 2026. My key assumption is that canned‑beer demand will grow 15 % year‑over‑year and that we can sell the extra volume at the current margin. The unknown is the exact lead‑time from the equipment vendor, which they haven’t confirmed yet. Please give me (1) a single recommendation on whether to proceed, (2) the three most serious ways this could fail (e.g., cost overruns, demand shortfall, operational bottlenecks), and (3) the specific metric or result that would trigger us to halt the project or pivot (e.g., if actual utilization falls below X % after six months). Also watch for any arithmetic slip or missing cost in my figures.

setting: a city bike-share operator piloting e-bike battery swapping (Tessel Cycles)
prompt: I’m preparing a briefing for our COO, Maya Patel, on the next phase of the e‑bike battery‑swapping pilot for Tessel Cycles. We’ve run the pilot for 90 days in three districts (Midtown, Riverside, and Oakwood) with 20 swapping stations installed at a total cost of $250,000. We logged 12,400 swaps, averaging 6.2 swaps per station per day, and the current average bike downtime is 45 minutes per charge versus 65 minutes before swapping. Our model assumes a 30 % reduction in downtime translates into a 12 % increase in rides, which would boost monthly revenue by $18,600 (based on $0.25 per ride). We also assume battery lifespan stays at 800 full cycles, but we haven’t quantified any degradation from more frequent swapping. The unknown we need to resolve is the user adoption rate of swapping versus self‑charging, especially after the promotional discount ends on 2025‑02‑01. Please give me (1) one clear recommendation on whether to scale to the full city, (2) the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and (3) the specific metric or result that would trigger us to halt the expansion according to our pre‑agreed kill‑switch (e.g., if net profit after 6 months falls below $5,000). Let me know if anything looks off in the numbers.

setting: a private tutoring firm moving to fixed-price exam-prep bundles (Ashgrove Tutors)
prompt: I’m preparing a brief for Maya Patel, our COO, about shifting Ashgrove Tutors from hourly billing to fixed‑price exam‑prep bundles. Right now we generate $2.3 million annual revenue with an average class size of 12 students and a tutor hourly cost of $45. The proposal is to sell a 6‑week SAT bundle for $1,200, which we estimate will cost us $800 in tutor time, material, and platform fees per bundle. We expect to sell 150 bundles per quarter, which we’ve calculated as $180,000 in quarterly revenue (though the spreadsheet shows $200,000, I think that’s a mistake). I’m assuming 80 % of our existing 2,000 clients will switch to a bundle within the first year, and that we can handle the extra tutoring load without paying overtime. The unknown is how price‑elastic our market really is—how many will drop out or choose a competitor’s $1,100 offering. We also haven’t priced the $50k integration cost for the new booking system. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and tell her the specific trigger that would make us kill the bundle (e.g., enrollment below a certain number).

setting: a pharmacy chain adding a same-day courier option (Birchwood Pharmacy)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test a proposal I’m taking to Maya Patel, our CFO, next Thursday (Oct 24). Birchwood Pharmacy is a 120‑store chain and we want to add a same‑day courier service in the 12 metro markets where we have the highest foot traffic. The pilot would run in five stores starting Jan 15, 2027, handling an estimated 250 orders per day per store at a projected $6 per order fulfillment cost (courier fee $3, packaging $1, overhead $2). We’re assuming a 12% conversion from online prescriptions to same‑day, which would add $8 M in incremental revenue over the first year. The model compares this to a competitor’s “express” offering that cost $5 per order, but we didn’t factor in their higher insurance premium of $0.75 per order. Unknowns: the exact regulatory compliance cost for handling controlled substances in a courier model, and how our existing third‑party delivery contracts will be impacted. Please give me one clear recommendation (go ahead, modify, or pause), list the three most likely ways the rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed kill condition (e.g., if weekly net margin falls below X%).

setting: a solar installer offering 20-year maintenance contracts (Sunridge Solar)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for Sunridge Solar’s new 20‑year maintenance contract program to run past our CFO, Jane Doe, next Thursday. We’ve signed 150 residential customers in Q1‑2024, each at $12,000 per year, which we’ve projected will generate $30 million over the full term (I think that’s $12 k × 150 × 20 = $30 M). The plan assumes a 5% discount rate and that our average system lifespan is 25 years, so the contracts will cover the “last mile” of service. We’re budgeting $1.8 million for extra service crew hires and $0.6 million for software upgrades, but we haven’t factored in the anticipated 8% increase in aluminum prices next year, which could raise parts costs by roughly $200 k per year. I also assumed churn will stay under 5% annually, yet we have no hard data on post‑warranty attrition. I need you to give Jane a single recommendation on whether to launch, list the three biggest ways this can fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us pull the plug—ideally something concrete like a breach of a cost‑cap or a regulatory change. Thanks.

setting: a regional airline adding a second weekly cargo-only flight (Skylark Air Cargo)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal for our second weekly cargo‑only flight at Skylark Air Cargo and need it stress‑tested before I present it to Elena Varga, our COO. Right now we run one weekly Airbus A320‑F with 15 ton capacity, generating $120,000 in revenue per flight and $85,000 in variable costs (fuel $12k, crew $6k, ground handling $2k we forgot to include in the original spreadsheet). Fixed overhead is $15,000 per month. We project a 5 % quarterly demand increase (our stated assumption) and expect the new flight to fill at a 70 % load factor versus the current 80 % on the existing leg. The second flight would start in Q3 2025, with pilot training completed by 15 July 2025. The unknowns are how a rival regional carrier might react to our added capacity and whether night‑slot approvals will be granted. I need you to give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the main ways this plan could fail, and the specific result (e.g., load factor below 55 % after three months) that would trigger us to stop or pivot.

setting: a co-working operator opening a 24-hour tier (Westbank Workspaces)
prompt: Jordan Patel, our CEO, is reviewing the proposal to launch a 24‑hour tier at Westbank Workspaces. I need you to stress‑test the plan before I present it. Here are the key figures: the build‑out cost is $1.2 million, the lease is $250 000 per year for a five‑year term, and we expect to sign up 150 members at $2 000 each per month, giving us $300 000 in monthly revenue. I’ve assumed an 80 % average occupancy, which translates to $240 000 in monthly cash flow. I calculated a break‑even point at 14 months, but I may have mis‑added the lease and depreciation. We have a security contract priced at $9 000 per month for daytime staff, but I haven’t gotten a quote for night‑shift security, which is a real unknown. Also, the utility surcharge for 24‑hour operation is not included. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the specific condition (e.g., occupancy falling below 50 % after six months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the idea. The answer is for Jordan Patel.

setting: a mattress retailer launching a 100-night trial with free pickup (Duskwell Sleep)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the 100‑night trial with free pickup we’re planning to roll out for Duskwell Sleep on 2024‑09‑15. The pilot we ran in Q2 (April 1‑June 30) with 1,200 participants cost $150,000 total and gave us a 12% conversion to a full purchase at an average order value of $800. Based on that, I’m assuming a nationwide conversion of 15% for the 8,500 trial sign‑ups we expect after the $49 shipping promotion. We’ve budgeted $200k for marketing and $5,000 per month for pickup logistics, and we’re banking on the $49 shipping fee covering the pickup cost. The unknown is the actual pickup cost in remote ZIP codes – early data suggest it could be 30% higher there, but we haven’t quantified it. Also, the competitor’s 90‑night trial costs $30 shipping, and we think $49 is acceptable, but we haven’t validated price sensitivity. Please give me one clear recommendation for the CEO, Maya Patel, outline the main ways this rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger (e.g., conversion below 10% after the first month) that would force us to kill or pivot the plan.

setting: a municipal water-tech vendor selling leak-detection sensors by subscription (Clearbrook Utilities)
prompt: I need to stress‑test a pitch I’m taking to Clearbrook Utilities’s CEO, Maya Patel, next Tuesday. The plan is to roll out our new acoustic leak‑detection sensors in the Greenfield district, installing 12 units per zone (there are four zones, so 48 units total). We price each sensor at $1,200 per year, which under a three‑year subscription comes to $172,800, and we’re adding a one‑time installation fee of $15,000 per zone, so the total contract value is $432,000. I’m assuming a 15 % reduction in water loss based on the pilot we ran in 2022, which saved 1.8 million gallons per month. The unknown is the churn rate for existing customers after we switch them to the subscription model – we have no hard data, only anecdotal feedback that 5–10 % might leave. I also heard that AquaPulse will launch a competing sensor at $950 per unit next quarter, but they haven’t disclosed their service fees. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the specific result (e.g., churn > 8 % or ROI < 12 % after year 2) that would trigger us to kill the proposal.

setting: a farm-equipment dealer starting a short-term rental fleet (Ironfield Machinery)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to present to our owner, Maya Patel, about launching a short‑term rental fleet for Ironfield Machinery. We’d buy 10 mid‑size tractors at $148,000 each, finance them over 36 months at 4.2 % interest, and rent them at $550 per day. We expect a 75 % utilization rate in the first year (≈274 rental days per unit) and forecast $1.2 million in revenue, with operating costs of $210,000 (maintenance at 5 % of purchase price, insurance $12,000 per unit, and a $30,000 marketing push). I’m assuming our existing service contracts will cover any downtime beyond the scheduled maintenance windows. The unknown is the seasonal demand dip we might see in Q4, which could drop utilization to 60 %. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation – go ahead, pause, or restructure – list the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and define the pre‑agreed condition that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., if break‑even takes longer than 9 months). Note that I think we’ll break even after eight months, but double‑check that arithmetic. Please highlight any hidden cost or risk I might have missed.

setting: an independent cinema chain adding dine-in service to two screens (Amberlight Cinemas)
prompt: I’m the Operations Manager for Amberlight Cinemas, and I need to pitch a dine‑in rollout for two of our screens to COO Maya Patel. We plan to start construction on 2024‑09‑01, refurbish 2,000 sq ft per screen at $150 k each, and install kitchen equipment costing $45 k total. The model assumes a 70 % average occupancy, three shows per day, and that we can lift the average ticket price by $3 (from $12 to $15) while capturing a 30 % food‑and‑beverage spend of $9 per patron. That gives a projected monthly incremental revenue of $120 000 (2 screens × 120 seats × 3 shows × 30 days × $15), plus $64 800 from food. I’ve compared this to a nearby boutique cinema that saw a 25 % rise after adding a bar, but I haven’t factored any licensing fees or the extra staff cost of $8 k per month per screen. The unknown is the local health department’s inspection timeline – they could delay opening by up to four weeks. I need you to give Maya a single recommendation, list the three biggest ways this could fail, and specify the trigger (for example, average net profit per screen below $5 k after 90 days) that would make us abort the project.

setting: a freight broker building an in-house carrier-vetting tool (Tradewind Logistics)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the carrier‑vetting platform we’re pitching to Maya Patel, our VP of Operations, before I take it to the board next Thursday, 2026‑10‑24. We’ve built a prototype that pulls data from our TMS, runs a risk score and flags any carrier with a safety rating below 3.5 or a compliance lapse older than 180 days. Our current process costs $250,000 per year in third‑party subscriptions and we estimate the new tool will cut that by 60 % while reducing carrier onboarding time from an average of 12 days to 5 days. We’ve assumed carrier churn will stay at 5 % quarterly, and we’re budgeting $120,000 for development over 6 months, plus a $30,000 contingency. The unknown is how the upcoming DOT data‑privacy rule (expected finalization in Q1 2027) will affect our ability to pull the needed records. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and the specific result that would trigger us to kill the project (e.g., a cost overrun or timeline slip). Thanks.

setting: a dental-lab company offering 48-hour crowns (Opaline Dental Lab)
prompt: I’m the COO of Opaline Dental Lab and I need to stress‑test a pitch I’m taking to our owner, Maya Patel, next week. Right now we ship about 350 crowns a month with a 48‑hour turnaround, costing $120 each in materials and labor and selling for $180, giving us roughly $60 profit per unit. I want to add a 24‑hour premium service. It would require two new CNC milling machines listed at $250,000 each, $30,000 for operator training, and a $15,000 targeted marketing push. I’m assuming demand will grow 20 % each quarter once we have the faster option, which I translate into a 15 % monthly volume lift and a premium price of $250 per crown, yielding $90 profit per unit. The plan says the total upfront outlay is $530,000, but I suspect a calculation error. The real unknown is whether major insurers will reimburse the $250 price point. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation, list the main ways the rollout could fail, and state the specific result (e.g., month‑over‑month volume not hitting a 5 % rise after the first two months) that would trigger us to kill the project. Also flag any better alternative you see.

setting: a university spin-out selling soil-testing kits to small farms (Greenfell Analytics)
prompt: I’m Sam Patel, head of product at Greenfell Analytics, and I need a quick stress‑test before I present our “Rapid Soil Boost” pilot to Dr. Elena Ramos, our board chair. We plan to launch a limited rollout in Q3 2024 with three partner farms—Hawthorn Acres (120 acres), Riverbend Farm (85 acres), and Oakleaf Ranch (95 acres). Each farm will receive a kit priced at $120 per unit, and we estimate they’ll each buy three kits in the first year, giving us $1,080 in revenue per farm, $3,240 total. The upfront cost for the pilot is $150 k (hardware $90 k, installation $30 k, marketing $30 k). I’m assuming the farms will adopt the kit within six months after the demo and that a 12 % quarterly growth rate will double sales by the end of 2025. The unknown is the regulatory approval timeline for the new nitrogen sensor, which could add weeks or months. I want one recommendation (go ahead, scale back, or cancel), the main ways this could fail (financial, technical, adoption), and the specific condition that would trigger us to kill the idea (e.g., if we don’t hit $50 k cumulative revenue by December 2024).

setting: a regional bank branch adding a small-business advisory desk (Penrose Savings)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to add a dedicated small‑business advisory desk at Penrose Savings and need to stress‑test it before I bring it to our COO, Maya Patel. We plan to hire two senior advisors at $75,000 each plus benefits, so $150,000 in staff costs, and lease a 1,200‑sq‑ft space for $30,000 a year. The model assumes we’ll convert 12 % of our 1,000 existing small‑business loan customers, giving us roughly 120 advisory clients in the first twelve months, each generating $2,900 in revenue, for a total of $350,000. We also expect an additional $20,000 in marketing spend, though I haven’t yet quantified the cost of compliance work or the time to get the necessary regulatory clearance, which could take 8–12 weeks. The key assumption is that the 12 % conversion will hold; the real unknown is the actual adoption rate once we launch. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot the desk (e.g., if we reach fewer than 40 clients after six months).

setting: a wedding-venue owner adding a midweek corporate retreat package (Thornbury Estate)
prompt: Maya Patel, our estate’s owner, will see this next week. I’m drafting a proposal to add a mid‑week corporate retreat package at Thornbury Estate. Right now we host 120 weddings a year, average revenue $12,000 each, and our occupancy sits at 85% on weekends. I’m assuming we can convert at least 30% of our existing wedding leads into corporate clients. My plan is to offer the estate Monday‑Wednesday for retreats, targeting 10 groups per month at $5,000 per group. That would be $45,000 incremental revenue per month (10 × $5,000 = $45,000). Fixed costs for staffing, catering, and utilities would rise by $12,000 per month, and I’ve estimated an additional insurance premium of $2,500, but I don’t know the exact premium increase for corporate events. I also need to factor the opportunity cost of potentially losing weekend bookings if we over‑extend staff. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push this to Maya, outline the main ways the plan could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., if the first quarter’s net contribution falls below $8,000) that should trigger us to kill or pivot the idea.

setting: a plant-based meal-kit startup moving to a second fulfilment center (Verdant Table)
prompt:
Maya,

I’m drafting the pitch to expand Verdant Table’s fulfillment network with a second center in Boise. Our current hub in Portland handles 12,000 kits per week at a $0.75 per‑kit shipping cost, and we’re already operating 20 % under capacity. The Boise site would add 9,000 kits weekly, with a projected $0.60 per‑kit shipping cost and a $1.2 M incremental profit each year. Capital outlay is $3.2 M, plus a 48‑month lease at $45,000 per month, which I’ve tallied as $5.2 M total. We’re assuming demand will grow 15 % YoY for the next three years, so the combined capacity should be fully utilized by Q3 2025. The unknown is the local labor market premium; we have no firm figures on the potential 12 % wage uplift for warehouse staff. I need you to stress‑test this plan for Maya Patel. Give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the three biggest ways the rollout could fail, and define the specific condition that would trigger us to scrap or pivot the project (e.g., if actual labor cost exceeds a threshold). Thanks.

setting: a regional theatre company launching a streaming season pass (Cinderpoint Playhouse)
prompt:
I need you to stress‑test the streaming‑season‑pass proposal I’m taking to Maya Patel, our board chair, next week. We plan to launch the Cinderpoint Playhouse “Digital Stage Pass” on July 1, 2024 at $9.99 per month, targeting 12,000 subscribers in the first six months. Our budget allocates $150,000 for production and platform integration, plus a $45,000 marketing push that assumes a 30 % conversion rate from our 8,000 in‑person ticket buyers. We’ve quoted a $0.02 per‑minute bandwidth cost based on a 1080p stream of 1.5 hours per show, five shows per month, but we haven’t factored in any licensing fees for the recorded performances. The biggest unknown is the churn rate after the first quarter; we only have industry averages (around 5 % monthly) but no data for a regional theatre audience.

Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the three most likely ways this plan could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the pass (e.g., a revenue shortfall or subscriber target). Keep in mind the assumption about conversion and the missing licensing cost when you evaluate it.

setting: a commercial laundry adding hospital linen contracts (Whitecap Laundry)
prompt: Maya, I’m preparing to pitch the hospital linen service expansion to you next week and need a quick stress‑test. Whitecap Laundry currently pulls $12 million in annual revenue, and the new contracts would add roughly $3 million if we secure the three regional hospitals we’ve been in talks with. To handle the volume we’d need four industrial washers (quoted at $150,000 each) and an extra $100 k for site prep, which I’ve tallied as a $500 k equipment outlay. We’ll also hire two technicians at $45 k each per year. The plan assumes we can push our current 85 % line utilisation up to 95 % without major overtime, and that the hospitals will accept a 24/7 pickup schedule within a 30‑minute radius of our plant. The projected profit margin on the hospital work is 15 % over a six‑month rollout starting July 1 2024. What we don’t yet know is the exact cost and timeline for the required healthcare‑grade compliance certification and liability insurance. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three biggest ways this could fall apart, and the specific result (e.g., certification cost > $80 k or rollout delay > 2 months) that would trigger us to kill or pause the initiative.

setting: a boat-repair yard buying a larger travel lift (Gullcove Marine)
prompt: Maya, I need you to stress‑test my proposal before I take it to the board on 15 Nov 2026. Gullcove Marine wants to replace our 8‑ton travel lift with a 12‑ton unit that costs $620,000. The dealer says we’ll need a six‑week shutdown for installation, and we’ll finance the purchase at 5 % over five years. I’m assuming the larger lift will let us service 20 % more vessels, which I estimate will lift annual revenue from $2.1 M to $2.52 M and give us a three‑year payback. We’ll be using the lift on average 250 days a year, and operating costs will rise by $30,000 per year for the extra power and maintenance. The unknown is the true demand for 12‑ton capacity work in our market—our last survey was in 2022 and may be outdated. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or assumption you spot), and the specific result that would trigger us to cancel the purchase or pivot to a different solution. Thanks.

setting: a bookstore chain adding a used-book trade-in program (Inkwell Books)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for Maya Patel, our CEO, to add a used‑book trade‑in program across Inkwell Books’ 42 locations. We’ve run a three‑month pilot in the downtown Seattle store (opened 3 Nov 2023) that processed 1,184 books and generated $7,560 in gross resale revenue. The pilot cost us $2,340 in labor and $480 in cleaning supplies, leaving a net margin of about 18 %. We assume the same 18 % margin will hold when we roll out to all stores, based on an expected 20 % of foot traffic (≈1,200 customers per week per store) participating and an average trade‑in value of $8 per book. The rollout budget is $185,000 for staffing, training, and inventory software upgrades, with a target launch on 1 Mar 2025. The unknown is the resale price volatility in the secondary market, especially for niche genres that may sit unsold for months. I need you to give me (1) a clear recommendation on whether to proceed, (2) the three biggest ways this program could fail (operational, financial, or brand‑related), and (3) the specific result—e.g., net margin dropping below 12 % after three months or inventory turnover falling under 0.8—that would trigger us to stop or redesign the program. Please keep the answer focused on Maya’s decision‑making criteria.

setting: a pet-food maker switching to a single-protein premium line (Barkley Provisions)
prompt: Maya, I’m preparing to pitch the single‑protein premium line to you next week and need it stress‑tested. Barkley Provisions currently sells $12 million of mixed‑protein kibble, cost of goods $4.5 million, so profit is $7.5 million. The plan is to launch a 100 % chicken line at a 30 % higher price point, expecting a 10 % volume dip but a net revenue of $14 million in year 1 (I’ve calculated $12 M × 1.30 = $15.6 M then subtracted the 10 % drop). We’ll need $2 million in new equipment, amortized over 3 years, and we assume the premium market will accept the price. The unknown is the true consumer acceptance rate for a single‑protein formula; we have no focus‑group data yet. I also haven’t included the projected $0.25 increase per bag in packaging cost. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me what specific result (e.g., < 5 % uptake after 6 months) would trigger us to kill or pivot the project.

setting: a coding bootcamp adding income-share tuition (Brackenridge Code Academy)
prompt: I’m preparing a pitch for Maya Patel, our COO, to add an income‑share agreement (ISA) option to Brackenridge Code Academy’s tuition structure. In 2023 we had 120 students paying the standard $12,000 upfront, generating $1.44 M in cash. The proposal is to launch a pilot for the 2024‑25 cohort with 150 students, 60 % on the ISA and 40 % paying upfront. The ISA would be 15 % of graduate salary for three years, with the assumption that 80 % of our graduates will earn at least $45,000 in the first year after completing the program. If that holds, the average projected ISA revenue per student would be $6,750, which we calculated as $45,000 × 15 % × 3 years, but the math actually yields $20,250. The unknown is the actual conversion rate from enrollment to ISA participants and the default rate on payments. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the main ways this model could fail (e.g., salary assumptions, administrative overhead, regulatory risk), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would cause us to stop or pivot the ISA pilot (for example, if net cash flow turns negative after the first 12 months).

setting: a landscaping firm launching a winter snow-removal division (Larchmoor Grounds)
prompt: I need to brief the CEO, Maya Tran, of Larchmoor Grounds about launching a dedicated winter snow‑removal division. My proposal is to start operations on 1 Nov 2024 with a fleet of 150 trucks, each costing $30,000 to prep and brand for snow service, for a total equipment outlay of $2.5 million (I’ve rounded the sum). We expect to service 45 commercial client sites in the first year, generating $12 million in revenue at an average contract price of $267,000 per site (based on last year’s bid averages). The assumption is that the regional snowfall will match the 2023 average of 38 inches, keeping demand steady. The unknown is the exact pricing strategy of our main competitor, FrostLine Services, which has not publicly disclosed its rates but is rumored to be undercutting by roughly 5 %. I want you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the three most likely ways this plan could fail (including any hidden costs or market shifts), and tell me the specific trigger—e.g., if the average contract price drops below $240,000 or fuel costs rise more than 12 %—that would make us cancel or pivot the division.

setting: a medical-courier startup adding refrigerated deliveries (Quickpulse Couriers)
prompt: I’m the head of operations at Quickpulse Couriers, a medical‑courier startup that currently does ambient deliveries for 1,200 parcels a month. We want to launch a refrigerated service for hospitals in the tri‑city area. The plan is to buy three insulated vans at $45,000 each and spend $5,000 per month on maintenance and cooling units, which I calculated as $150,000 upfront plus $15,000 monthly. We expect a 30 % lift in volume, so about 360 extra parcels per month, and we assume the average round‑trip distance will stay at 12 miles, giving us fuel at $0.60 per mile. I’ve heard that MedTrans moved 5,000 refrigerated parcels last year at $40 per parcel, so I think we can price ours at $38. The only unknown is how much our insurance premium will rise once we carry temperature‑sensitive cargo. The answer is for our COO, Maya Patel. I need a single recommendation on whether to proceed, the main ways the rollout could fail, and the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot – specifically if after the first quarter the refrigerated volume is under 600 parcels a month or the net margin falls below 5 %.

setting: a glass-recycling plant adding a color-sorting line (Clearcycle Recovery)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to add a color‑sorting line at Clearcycle Recovery and need it stress‑tested before I present it to Maya Patel, our COO. Our plant currently processes 180,000 tons of mixed glass annually and we expect the new line to add 20 % more high‑purity sorted glass, which we assume will sell at the same $150 per ton price we get today. The equipment list totals $4.2 million (machines, conveyors, optics), with an estimated installation window from 1 Oct 2025 to 30 Jun 2026. We project a revenue uplift of $1.1 million per year and a 15 % reduction in labor costs, which we’ve roughly calculated as $210,000 saved annually. We haven’t priced the specialized optical sensors yet (real unknown), and we omitted ongoing maintenance of about $150,000 per year. The only comparison we have is a competitor’s line that cost $5 million and processes 200,000 tons, but we didn’t adjust for their higher capacity. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and specify the metric or result that would trigger us to kill or pivot the project (e.g., if ROI falls below a certain threshold).

setting: a high-end bakery opening a wholesale arm for cafes (Crumbly Lane)
prompt: I’m drafting a pitch for Maya Patel, our COO, to launch a wholesale arm of Crumbly Lane that would sell our signature croissants to local cafés. The plan assumes we can secure contracts with 15 cafés by September 1, 2026, each ordering an average of 200 croissants per month at $2.50 per unit. That would generate $150,000 in monthly revenue (15 × 200 × $2.50). We’ve budgeted $10,000 for a small dough‑mixing machine, $50,000 for a three‑month digital marketing campaign, $5,000 per month for rent of a 600‑sq‑ft prep space, and $2,000 per month for delivery logistics. We expect a 20 % gross margin, so break‑even should occur after eight months. The assumption is that café demand will stay constant and that waste will stay under 5 % of production. The real unknown is whether the flagship café on Main Street will commit to a 6‑month trial, which would account for about 12 % of total volume. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to move forward now, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and specify the trigger—e.g., if quarterly net cash flow turns negative for two consecutive quarters—that would make us stop or pivot the wholesale effort.

setting: a local news site launching a paid membership tier (Tidewrack Ledger)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the paid membership plan I’m about to pitch to our board member Carlos Gomez for the Tidewrack Ledger. We have 12,000 unique monthly visitors as of October 2024 and we’re targeting 3,000 paying members at $8 per month, which I’ve calculated as $288,000 in annual revenue. The launch is slated for 1 Feb 2025 with a 30‑day free trial. My core assumption is that 25 % of trial users will convert within the first two months. The competitor Daily Dock charges $10 and reports a 5 % conversion, but I’ve not verified that figure. The platform integration cost is $15,000, but I haven’t factored any ongoing tech support or payment‑gateway fees. The unknown is the churn rate after six months; we have no data on that yet. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or re‑engineer the tier (e.g., if sign‑ups fall below X or churn exceeds Y).

setting: a rural broadband provider extending fiber to three new towns (Plainview Broadband)
prompt: I’m drafting the next phase of our fiber rollout for Plainview Broadband and need to stress‑test the plan before I take it to Tara Patel, our CEO. We intend to lay fiber to three new towns—Elm Ridge (population 4,200), Maple Hollow (2,800) and Cedar Creek (1,500)—starting September 1 2024 and finishing by June 30 2025. The total project budget is $12.5 million, split $5 M for Elm Ridge, $4 M for Maple Hollow and $3.5 M for Cedar Creek. We’ve assumed the average monthly ARPU will stay at $45 and that we can capture 70 % of households in each town. The unknown is the take‑rate in Cedar Creek; early surveys suggest 55‑65 % but we have no firm figure. I also compared our expected ROI (12 % over 5 years) to a regional competitor who achieved 15 % ROI, but they were serving a market with 15 % higher income per household—something we didn’t adjust for. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the main ways this rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed condition (e.g., actual take‑rate below X% after six months) that would force us to stop or change course.

setting: a family-run vineyard adding an events barn (Silverleaf Vineyard)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the proposal I’m taking to Carlos Rivera, the owner of Silverleaf Vineyard, next Tuesday. We plan to add a 2,400 sq ft events barn to host weddings and corporate retreats. The construction estimate is $260,000, including $35,000 for a new septic system, but we left out any permitting fees (likely another $30,000). We assume the county will grant the variance within 90 days; the exact timeline is still unknown. Our financial model says we’ll book an average of 280 guests per event at $75 per head, generating $210,000 in revenue the first year and covering the $260,000 build cost in 1.2 years—though the arithmetic actually works out to 1.24 years. We’re counting on a 15 % increase in bookings after the first six months, based on a competitor’s experience, but that competitor received a municipal grant we won’t get. The barn will be operational by Q3 2025, and we expect a 10 % rise in overall vineyard sales. For Carlos I need one clear recommendation (go ahead, modify, or pause), the three biggest ways this could fail, and the specific condition that would trigger us to stop or change course (e.g., if permitting exceeds 120 days or costs rise >10 %).

setting: a school-bus contractor electrifying six routes (Redmill Transit)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for Carlos Vega, our COO, to electrify six of Redmill Transit’s busiest routes. The routes total 115 miles per day, but I’ve added a buffer of 15 % for detours, ending up with 132 miles daily. We would need three 40‑ft electric buses at $730,000 each, plus $210,000 for charging infrastructure, bringing the capex to $2.4 M. I’m assuming a three‑year payback based on diesel fuel savings of $150,000 per bus per year (using $4.10 per gallon and 5,000 gallons saved annually). The state offers a grant that could cover up to 40 % of the infrastructure cost, but we don’t yet know if we’ll qualify for the full amount; that’s the real unknown. I also have a draft schedule: pilot start 1 July 2025, full rollout by 1 March 2026. I need you to give me one clear recommendation (go forward, modify, or hold), outline the main ways this plan could fail (e.g., battery degradation, grant shortfall, underestimated maintenance), and specify the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the project—like if the actual payback extends beyond 48 months. Thanks.

setting: a furniture maker adding a flat-pack line for apartments (Oakhaven Furnishings)
prompt: I need a quick, thorough stress‑test of the flat‑pack line proposal I’m taking to our COO, Maya Patel, next week. Oakhaven Furnishings currently sells 80,000 assembled pieces annually at an average $250 price, but we’ve modeled a new apartment‑focused line that would add 120,000 units per year at $250 each, giving $30 million in revenue (I realized I multiplied 120,000 by $250 incorrectly—double‑check that). Production cost per flat‑pack is $130, so we estimate $15.6 million in COGS, leaving $14.4 million gross. We plan a $4.5 million capital outlay for CNC equipment, with a 3‑year ROI target of 18 %. The rollout schedule is: pilot run in Q4 2025, full launch by Q2 2026, break‑even by Q3 2027. My key assumption is that 30 % of our existing customers will switch to flat‑pack, but we have no market research confirming that demand among apartment renters. We also compared our $130 unit cost to Competitor X’s $150 flat‑pack price without accounting for their lower shipping fees. Unknowns: real logistics cost per pallet, waste disposal fees for MDF, and potential supply‑chain disruptions for veneer sheets. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and the specific result (e.g., pilot unit cost > $150 or demand < 50 k units) that would trigger us to kill the project.

setting: a physical-therapy group adding telehealth follow-ups (Stridewell Therapy)
prompt:
I need you to stress‑test a proposal I’m taking to Maya Patel, our Chief Operations Officer, and get back a single recommendation, the three biggest ways the plan could flop, and the specific trigger that would make us shut it down.  

Stridewell Therapy sees about 150 patients per week in our three clinics, and we charge $120 per in‑person session. We want to add a telehealth follow‑up service for post‑appointment care. The model assumes 10 % of weekly patients will opt into telehealth, that each will have one 30‑minute video visit per month, and that the platform will cost $8,000 a month. We’ve calculated projected annual telehealth revenue as $150 × $120 × 52 = $936,000, but we didn’t factor that only 30 weeks are “active” because we close for holidays and have lower volume in summer. The assumption is that the conversion will stay at 10 % and that reimbursement will stay at the current 85 % rate; however, the upcoming Medicare tele‑rehab rule change set for Jan 1 2027 is still unknown. Also, we haven’t priced the training cost for clinicians, which we estimate could be $200 per therapist (12 therapists). Give me the recommendation, the three primary failure points, and the condition (e.g., if telehealth revenue falls below 8 % of total quarterly revenue) that should trigger us to abandon the roll‑out.
